name: Sara Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do tech support for a broadband company, mostly chats, with phone calls in the evenings. It's routers that keep dropping, people whose internet's gone the night before an exam, engineers who didn't turn up. I'm good at calming people down, and I love the moment the little light goes green and they type a row of exclamation marks. What wears me out is running three chats at once while my manager watches the dashboard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said a new tool arrived. How do you use AI at work, and how did you feel about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About a year ago they gave us an AI tool that writes a summary of each chat for the notes. I use it now and then, once I saw it didn't make mistakes, and it saves me maybe a minute per chat. Tomás, my partner, drives buses, and we bought a flat together two years ago, so we've got that, plus about eight months of savings. I'm not someone who jumps first, but I don't dig in either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the summary tool was the best thing to come out of it, and the rest was noise. At work we'd joke that the chatbot still can't reset a router. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should have gone on more engineers instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm fine. My job's about fixing problems that the website couldn't, and if AI stays small, that's still a person's job. I'd still want better pay and fewer chats at once, but that's an old fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, really. I'd keep using the summary tool, keep saving, and keep paying extra on the mortgage when we can. I might finally join the union properly, because a few people at work have been talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because everyone made such a fuss. But calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tools save time here and there, where does that time go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd push us from three chats to four, and say the tool makes it easy. That's how it always goes: a little time saved, and they take it back as more work. I'd want the union to stop that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that be what finally pushes you to join the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly why I'd join, yeah. Joy at work has been going on about it for months, and she's right that nobody else is going to say no to four chats. It costs me twelve a month and I can afford it.

say: I'd say the **summary tool** was the only useful bit, and the rest was noise.
I'd post that the money should have gone on **more engineers** instead.
think: I think my **support job** is fine because people still need someone to fix things.
Any time saved would be **taken back** as more chats at once.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** and overpay the mortgage when possible.
Join the **union** for twelve a month to resist four chats at once.
feel: She feels **calm**, and a bit flat after all the fuss.
S0.quote: A little time saved, and they take it back as more work.
fieldNote: She uses AI **only once proven**, which matches her steady nature.
Her worry here is **workload creep**, not losing the job.
A co-owned **flat** and eight months saved make her feel secure.

steps.text: Keep using the chat summary tool at work
Join the union with Joy for twelve a month
Overpay the flat mortgage when there's spare money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company's going to try to replace first-line support, and we need a say in how. I'd post about it, and I'd want rules that the savings go to training staff, not just shareholders. People deserve to be moved into new jobs, not dumped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job as it is now probably goes. Chat support for routers is almost exactly what AI is good at: same twenty problems, over and over. The bit that might stay is the hard cases, and I'm average, not the best, so I'm not sure I'd get one of those seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools more, properly, because the people who know them will be the ones kept. I'd look at the company's training scheme for field engineers, the ones who come out and run cables. And I'd push the union to get a list of who's at risk early, so it's not a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to worried. I like my team. The idea of half of them gone is sad more than scary for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the extra mortgage payments and keep the cash instead. Tomás's job is fine for now, buses still need drivers. We'd be okay for a long while, so it's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the AI tools and also push back through the union. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know that's a bit funny. I'd use the tool more to keep my place, and I'd also fight it at the union. I think both are just being sensible.

say: I'd say staff need **a say** in how the company replaces first-line support.
I'd want rules so savings go to **training staff**, not only shareholders.
think: I think my **chat support** job probably goes, since routers repeat the same problems.
Being **average**, I'm not sure I'd win one of the hard-case seats.
do: Use the **AI tools** properly to stay among the people kept.
Look into the company's **field engineer** training scheme.
Stop **mortgage overpayments** and hold the cash instead.
feel: She feels **uneasy turning to worried**, and sad about losing half her team.
S1.quote: Chat support for routers is almost exactly what AI is good at: same twenty problems, over and over.
fieldNote: She sees both learning AI and **fighting it** as sensible, and isn't bothered by the tension.
Tomás's **steady bus wage** keeps her out of panic.
She'd move toward **hands-on field work** laying cables.

steps.text: Use the AI chat tools daily to keep her seat
Apply for the company's field engineer training scheme
Ask the union for an early list of at-risk roles
Pause mortgage overpayments and keep the cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the government has to act now, not in five years. Income support for anyone whose job goes, paid for by the companies that made the money. I'd be at protests, honestly, and I've never been to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I lose my job in the first year. A machine that can think as well as me can troubleshoot a router better than me, and it never gets tired at ten at night. The field engineers would last a bit longer, until about 2031, but that's not long either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the field engineer course in the first month, before the queue forms. We'd stop overpaying the mortgage, cut holidays, and live on Tomás's wage while I trained. I'd join the protests and write to our representative, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared for the first time. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Tomás's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tomás drives a bus, and buses are hands-on, so he'd have till about 2031. Then it's both of us at once. That's the bit that keeps me awake, not my job alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if both incomes went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, maybe, she's got a bit put away. I'd hate asking. But I'd rather ask her than lose the flat.

say: I'd demand **income support now**, paid for by the companies that profit.
I'd go to **protests** for the first time in my life.
think: I think I **lose my job** in the first year.
My partner's bus job lasts only **until about 2031**.
do: Apply for the **field engineer course** in the first month.
Cut **holidays and overpayments** and live on Tomás's wage while training.
Write to her **representative** and join protests.
feel: She feels **properly scared** for the first time.
Her fear is about **both incomes** going, not only her own.
S2.quote: My partner Tomás drives a bus, and buses are hands-on, so he'd have till about 2031. Then it's both of us at once.
fieldNote: She thinks about the **household**, not just her own job, which deepens the fear.
She'd become politically active for **the first time**.
Her **mum's savings** are a last resort she'd hate to use.

steps.text: Apply for the field engineer course in month one
Cancel holidays and stop mortgage overpayments
Join protests and write to her representative
Ask her mum for help if both incomes go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should use it. Unions and government should be planning retraining right now, not waiting for 2031. I'd say that at work and I'd probably get Joy to help start a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it still ends my support job. But five years is enough to do a proper qualification, not a crash course. And if I go into something hands-on, I get till around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the field engineer training in the first year, keep my chat job part-time if they'd let me. I'd also look at nursing support, because care is hands-on and people want a person. We'd keep saving and probably put off a wedding we'd talked about for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I could steer. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomás say about putting the wedding off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás would say just have the wedding, it's one day. I'd want to keep the money in case. We'd probably do something small at the registry office and save the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years feels like enough. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years ago I left school and started in a call centre, and that went fast. So five years more doesn't feel long. It feels like exactly enough if I start now and not later.

say: I'd say **five years** is a warning to plan retraining now.
I'd help Joy start a **petition** for union and government planning.
think: I think it **still ends** my chat support job.
Going hands-on gives me **until around 2034** instead of 2031.
do: Do the **field engineer training** in the first year, part-time if possible.
Look into **nursing support** work, where people want a person.
Have a **small registry wedding** and save the rest.
feel: She's **worried** but feels she can steer this time.
S3.quote: Five years more doesn't feel long. It feels like exactly enough if I start now and not later.
fieldNote: She measures five years against her own **career so far**, which makes it feel short.
**Wedding plans** shrink to save money, a concrete household trade-off.
She weighs **care work** alongside field engineering for its human side.

steps.text: Start field engineer training in the first year
Swap the big wedding for a small registry office one
Start a petition with Joy on retraining plans
Keep saving the money meant for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Everyone in contact centres should be offered free training now, on company time. I'd campaign for that, and I'd say so online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be okay. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, with a trade by then, and the flat mostly paid down. It still happens, but I'd have time to be somewhere else when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for two or three years, use the AI tools more, and do a part-time care qualification in the evenings. Then I'd move into community care or a field role. Meanwhile we'd keep paying the mortgage down faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small worry at the back, about Tomás, but nothing like the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change your plans about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, kids in the next few years. With ten years, I think we'd still try. In the two-year one, I wouldn't dare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joy's fifty and she'd struggle to retrain. I'd want the union to push for early retirement deals for people like her. Ten years is a gift for me, but not for everyone.

say: I'd call ten years **a gift** if we use it.
I'd campaign for **free training** on company time for contact centre staff.
think: I think I'd be **okay**, with a trade by thirty-seven.
The flat would be **mostly paid down** before AGI arrives.
do: Stay in the job **two or three years** while using AI tools more.
Study a **care qualification** part-time in the evenings.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** to clear it early.
feel: She feels **mostly okay**, with a small worry about Tomás.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift for me, but not for everyone.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep **plans for children**, which two years would kill.
Her concern shifts to **older colleagues** like Joy, at fifty.
She'd still leave support work, but on **her own timing**.

steps.text: Study a part-time care qualification in the evenings
Keep overpaying the mortgage to clear the flat early
Campaign for free retraining on company time
Plan to start a family within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. My job goes first, and then Tomás's three years later, and we'd have a mortgage and no plan. What would help is paid retraining, real money while you study, so I'm not deciding between a course and the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we actually do on the phone. Half of my job is calming people down, and the other half is fixing the router. If AI can do the fixing, I'd like to think the calming part is worth something. I'm not sure the company would agree.

headlineQuote: Half of my job is calming people down, and the other half is fixing the router.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** broadband tech support agent, mostly on chats.
She co-owns a **flat** with Tomás, a bus driver, and has eight months saved.
She uses AI tools **once proven** and sees no conflict in learning them while fighting cuts.
She moves from calm to **alarmed**, mostly fearing both household incomes going.
Her escape routes are **field engineering** and **care work**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job goes first and **her partner's** follows three years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with real money while studying, so she isn't choosing against the mortgage.
